content: Hammer toe is a condition characterized by a deformity of the toe, where the end of the toe bends downward, creating an abnormal shape. The middle joint of the toe becomes bent, and the tip of the toe points downward, resembling a claw-like deformity. Initially, the toe may still be flexible, allowing movement and straightening. However, as the condition progresses, the toe becomes rigid and immobile. Corns often develop on the top of the affected toe due to friction, and calluses may form on the sole of the foot. Walking or wearing shoes can become increasingly painful as the deformity worsens. Hammer toe most commonly affects the second toe, although other toes can also be involved. The deformity occurs when the toe is forced into a bent position, often due to wearing shoes that are too short, narrow, or tight. Over time, the muscles and tendons in the toe tighten and shorten, leading to the claw-like position. In some cases, hammer toe may be congenital (present at birth) or develop gradually over time. Rarely, all toes may be affected, which could indicate an underlying issue with the nerves or spinal cord. Certain groups are at higher risk of developing hammer toe. Women who frequently wear poorly fitting shoes or high heels are more susceptible. Children who continue to wear shoes they have outgrown are also at increased risk. A diagnosis of hammer toe is typically made through a physical examination of the foot. A healthcare provider will observe the deformity and assess the range of motion in the affected toes. Decreased and painful movement in the toes is a common finding. It is important to seek medical care if you have hammer toe, especially if the pain worsens or if walking becomes difficult. A healthcare provider can provide guidance on the most appropriate treatment options. Treatment for hammer toe depends on the severity of the condition. In mild cases, particularly in children, the affected toe can be treated with manual manipulation and splinting. Adjustments in footwear can also help alleviate symptoms. Wearing properly sized shoes with wide toe boxes can prevent further aggravation of the deformity. Corn pads or felt pads can protect the protruding joint. For additional support, a podiatrist can provide custom foot devices, such as hammer toe regulators or straighteners, which are also available for purchase over the counter. Gentle stretching exercises may be beneficial if the toe is not yet fixed in position. For example, picking up a towel with the toes can help stretch and strengthen the small muscles in the foot. In severe cases, surgical intervention may be necessary to correct the deformity. Surgery typically involves cutting or repositioning tendons and ligaments to straighten the joint. In some instances, the bones on either side of the joint may need to be fused together. Most patients can return home on the same day as the surgery. However, the affected toe may remain stiff or shorter following the procedure. If treated early, hammer toe can often be managed without surgery, reducing pain and improving mobility. However, untreated hammer toe can lead to complications, such as permanent foot deformity or changes in posture due to difficulty walking. To prevent hammer toe, it is essential to wear shoes that fit properly and provide adequate space for the toes. Regularly checking children’s shoe sizes, especially during periods of rapid growth, can help prevent the condition from developing.
